title: Swiss meringue buttercream
subtitle: The smooth, stable frosting made by heating egg whites and sugar before beating
excerpt: Swiss meringue buttercream starts by dissolving sugar into egg whites over heat, then whipping to a stiff meringue before adding butter in pieces. The result is silky, far less sweet than American buttercream, and stable enough for piping flowers and coating tiered cakes.
sourceNotes: Swiss meringue buttercream is a standard professional patisserie product taught across culinary training programmes. The name comes from the Swiss meringue method (heating egg whites with sugar before beating), which predates American meringue (no heating) and Italian meringue (hot sugar syrup) as a stabilising approach. The formula described here is standard.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge, then bring to room temperature and beat again until smooth.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles cleanly; use a larger bowl and ensure the stand mixer bowl is large enough for the full meringue volume.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Store at room temperature for 2 days or in the fridge for 1 week. Re-beat before use.

glossaryTerms.definition: A meringue made by warming egg whites and sugar together over a bain-marie until the sugar dissolves completely, then whipping to stiff peaks. More stable than French meringue (unheated whites) because the gentle heat denatures some of the egg protein.
A bowl of ingredients set over a pan of simmering water. The indirect heat warms the contents gently and evenly without the risk of scrambling or scorching.

content.text: Swiss meringue buttercream takes about 30 minutes from start to finish and requires a stand mixer; doing it by hand is not practical. The

base dissolves the sugar completely before the whites are beaten, which is why the finished buttercream is smooth and never gritty. The butter goes in cold and in small pieces; adding it too fast breaks the emulsion.

items.prepNote: cut into 2 cm cubes, cold from the fridge

content.text: Combine the egg whites and caster sugar in the stand mixer bowl. Set it up as a
: place the bowl over a pan of simmering water. The bowl must not touch the water.

Stir constantly with a spatula until the sugar has completely dissolved and the mixture reaches 70 to 72 degrees Celsius on an instant-read thermometer. If you do not have a thermometer, rub a small amount between your fingers: it should feel completely smooth with no grit. This takes 8 to 10 minutes.

Transfer the bowl to the stand mixer. Beat on high speed with the whisk attachment until the meringue holds stiff peaks and the bowl has cooled to room temperature. This takes 10 to 15 minutes. The bowl must feel cool before the butter goes in.
Switch to the paddle attachment and reduce the speed to medium. Add the cold butter cubes one or two at a time, waiting for each addition to be incorporated before adding the next. Do not rush this.
The mixture will look curdled and soupy about halfway through. This is normal. Keep adding butter and beating; it will come together into a smooth, silky cream as the last cubes go in.
Add the salt and vanilla extract and beat for a further 2 minutes until fully combined. Taste and adjust.

If the buttercream stays liquid after all the butter is added, the bowl is too warm. Place it in the fridge for 10 minutes, then beat again. If it looks curdled and will not come together, the butter was too cold. Set the bowl briefly over a gentle heat for 30 seconds and beat again.
